reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The Statcast batting card sits at .411 xwOBA and .563 xSLG, both 98th percentile, with a 15.2% walk rate that explains the gap between what he does and what pitchers want him to do. The contact side has a real cost, a 28.5% whiff rate, but when he connects, 52.1% of balls are hard-hit and he barrels 16.5% of them, so the damage is not in question. On the mound, a 2.70 xERA and 30.4% whiff rate build the case that this isn't a gimmick, though his 7.6% walk rate as a pitcher is the lever to watch: if command tightens, the pitching side becomes a genuine asset on top of everything else; if it balloons, it becomes a high-strikeout arm propped up by stuff alone. The projection at .397 OBP, .546 SLG, 38 home runs across 691 plate appearances is the floor if the bat stays what the Statcast numbers say it is.

reports.published_report: A 22.8% barrel rate and a 17.5% walk rate on the same card is the argument, full stop. The contact limits are genuine: pitchers are beating him inside the zone, not outside it, because a 31.1% whiff rate sits against a 22.4% chase rate. But when Wood makes contact, the .615 xSLG says what kind of contact it is. If pitchers find the in-zone sequence that exposes the whiff rate at scale, the projection's .265/.389/.523 line compresses; if the 17.5% walk rate holds, he has enough margin to absorb a 28.9% strikeout rate and still be a middle-of-the-order force at 23.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-five projected home runs from a 22-year-old third baseman who already owns a 93.1 mph average exit velocity and a 51.1% hard-hit rate is the kind of profile that makes the age feel like the most dangerous part of the sentence. The contact quality is already there — the .366 xwOBA and .497 xSLG aren't running ahead of what the bat speed and barrel rate can sustain, and a 12.5% walk rate that would be elite for a veteran gives the .275/.356/.538 projection a real floor. The one lever that could flatten the ceiling is the fielding OAA sitting at the 1st percentile; if Tampa decides the defensive cost at third is too steep and moves him, the profile at a different position is a different conversation. For now, he's on track to be one of the more complete offensive seasons in the American League, at an age when most players are still figuring out a level.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .312, which is the cleanest single number in his Statcast profile, and it sits at the 100th percentile. That's the foundation: he makes contact at an elite level and hits it as hard as almost anyone, with a 93.3 mph average exit velocity and 52.7% hard-hit rate both checking in around the 95th percentile. The one tension worth naming is a 33.0% chase rate, which keeps his plate discipline from matching his contact quality, and if pitchers ever find a way to exploit it more consistently, the batting average comes down with it. If they don't, the projection at .290/.358/.478 with 47 stolen bases at shortstop is a description of a genuine MVP-caliber season, not a ceiling.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .368 xwOBA and 49.6% hard-hit rate say the bat is ahead of where his raw numbers landed — a 24-year-old who makes loud contact and runs at 29.4 ft/s is a problem for outfields. The tension is the chase rate. At 36.1%, pitchers have a reliable door into his swing, and that 25.5% strikeout rate is the ceiling's load-bearing wall: if he can't tighten that up, the projections (.279/.359/.510, 33 home runs, 38 steals over 686 plate appearances) stay optimistic on paper. He's already the kind of player who can beat you six different ways; the question is whether his plate discipline matures into something that turns a very good player into a true lineup anchor rather than one who gets exploited in October counts.

When Kurtz makes contact, 58.9% of it is hard-hit and he's barreling at 18.3%, both sitting at the very top of the league, and an 18.6% walk rate that is historically elite means he's getting on base regardless of what pitchers do with his chase tendencies. The .382 xwOBA tells you the production is sustainable across a meaningful sample; the .251 xBA sitting against that tells you the walks and power are doing most of the carrying, which is fine when the power is this extreme. If the strikeout rate climbs further and pitchers find a way to suppress the walk rate simultaneously, the floor drops fast, but if it holds, you're looking at a true middle-of-the-order force, and the projected .906 OPS is the conservative read on where that combination of patience and raw power lands.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.74 and the ERA projection settles at 3.32 over 182.888 innings — the gap between those two numbers is the whole argument for why the surface results still understate him. His strikeout rate of 29.3% and walk rate of 5.5% combine to form a command-to-stuff profile that almost never cracks in translation to a full season, and an xwOBA against of .259 confirms hitters aren't squaring him up even when they make contact. The one wrinkle is that his whiff rate of 27.8% trails what you'd expect from a pitcher getting this many strikeouts, which means the chase rate, 33.5%, is doing more of the heavy lifting than pure swing-and-miss; if hitters tighten their zone discipline against him, the strikeout total bears the cost first.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.peak_summary: Projection: impact everyday bat with high risk. The current bat shape is impact over 232 PA.
reports.published_report: The .416 OBP at 18 years old, across 339 plate appearances split between A and A+, is the number that frames everything else. Willits is walking at an 18% clip that translates to a 12.0% MLB-equivalent rate, more than three points above the big-league average, while the 12 home runs and .217 ISO against A-ball arms hint at real bat-to-ball and emerging pop together. The 38 steals sit behind all of it as a reminder that this is a shortstop who can hurt you four ways. If the strike-zone discipline holds as he climbs and the ISO doesn't evaporate when the pitching quality rises, he becomes an impact everyday bat; if the K% that already translates above league average ticks further in the wrong direction, this becomes a good-contact, high-OBP regular rather than a true middle-of-the-order piece.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact-quality case for De La Cruz is almost absurd: 94.4 mph average exit velocity at the 99th percentile, a 52.8% hard-hit rate, and a .363 xwOBA that the underlying power shape fully supports. The problem is a 29.1% whiff rate that drags strikeouts to 28.7%, and the whole profile hinges on whether he can keep that chase rate (26.4%, respectable) low enough to let the damage play rather than get nullified by swing-and-miss in the zone. If he does, the projection lands at .268/.346/.479 with 26 home runs and 29 stolen bases, which is a legitimately dangerous all-around shortstop season. If the whiff rate climbs, you still have the speed and the raw power, but the batting average bleeds and the value thins toward a boom-or-bust regular rather than a star.

reports.name: Corbin Carroll
reports.published_report: The 29.1% whiff rate is the one thing standing between this profile and a true star line. Everything else in the Statcast card points toward an above-average regular: 91.3 mph average exit velocity, 11.5% barrels, a walk rate near the top quarter of the league, and sprint speed at the 97th percentile that makes every ball in play a genuine event. The contact-avoidance problem cuts against a strikeout rate of 22.4% — he's getting away with it in the box score for now, but the xwOBA of .348 and the projection's .841 OPS across 674 plate appearances say the overall offensive picture is already well above replacement. If he ever tightens the swing-and-miss, this becomes a 24-homer, 21-steal guy who hits near the top of a playoff lineup; if the whiff rate climbs and pitchers adjust, you're still looking at a useful everyday outfielder whose legs and defense keep him valuable.

reports.name: Max Clark

reports.published_report: The contact rates are doing the heavy lifting here. At AAA over 357 PA, Clark is striking out at 14% while walking at 11%, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his K% at 17.8, well below the MLB mean of 22.0, with his walk rate at 9.7%, comfortably above 8.5%. reports.name: Cristopher Sánchez
reports.published_report: A 38.4% chase rate is the engine here, and it runs cleaner than almost anyone in the league. Sánchez doesn't blow hitters away, his hard-hit and barrel numbers sit well below average, but he doesn't need to when batters are swinging at that many pitches outside the zone, and when he walks just 4.8% of them, he never gives the game back. The 32.3% whiff rate fills in what the contact profile concedes: the stuff plays, even if the raw velo isn't the story. reports.name: Bryce Harper
reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .399 and the xSLG is .530, and those two numbers are doing something unusual: they're running well ahead of a 90.1 mph average exit velocity that ranks middling by Statcast standards. What Harper has is discipline that most hitters would trade a tick of bat speed for, a 15.1% walk rate that almost nobody matches, paired with a chase rate low enough to keep pitchers honest and a strikeout rate that barely registers as a problem at 20.2%. The swing-and-miss numbers are ugly in isolation, a 30.5% whiff rate that looks like exposure, but the walks suppress the damage and the barrel rate backs the slugging. If the contact quality dips or the plate discipline erodes with age, the profile gets thinner fast, because the exit velocity doesn't leave a safety net. As long as the eye stays sharp, the projection's .371 OBP and 33 home runs across 678 plate appearances are where this lands.

reports.peak_summary: Projection: back end starter with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 56 IP.
reports.published_report: The strikeout stuff is loud — 12.1 K/9 at AA, translating to 9.3 against major-league hitters, which sits above a league average of 8.6, but the walks are eating the profile alive. Thirty-three free passes in 56 innings, translating to 4.6 walks per nine in an MLB context where the baseline is 3.2, leaves a K-BB% that barely reaches league average once you run it through the converter. The skill shape here is a 70-grade miss sitting on top of 30-grade command, and that combination either forces a relief conversion or demands a significant mechanical correction before the ETA window of one to two years closes. If the walks come down, there's a back-end starter; if they don't, what's left is a depth arm who strikes guys out and nothing else.

reports.name: Griffin Jax
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a puzzle with one loud piece and one ugly one. His 31.5% whiff rate and 33.7% chase rate say he can miss bats at a meaningful level, and 2526 rpm on his fastball spin sits at the 95th percentile, which explains how the swing-and-miss generates. The problem is what happens when contact lands: a 10.9% barrel rate and an xERA of 5.10 say hitters are doing serious damage when they connect, and that gap between a projected 3.67 ERA and the underlying contact quality is the whole tension in the profile. If Jax can keep hitters off the barrel while living off the chase and whiff numbers he's already producing, the 3.67 ERA version holds; if not, you're looking at a high-leverage reliever whose stuff plays better in shorter stints where the barrel luck can't accumulate.

reports.name: Jacob deGrom
reports.published_report: The tension in this profile is right there in the contact numbers: a 34.4% whiff rate sitting next to a 44.0% hard-hit rate and an average exit velocity of 90.7 mph. That's a pitcher who misses bats at an elite level but gets hurt when hitters do connect, and the xERA of 3.44 is roughly where the two forces settle. The strikeout rate at 30.4% and a walk rate of just 5.5% mean he's still commanding the zone the way only a handful of starters can, and at 97.2 mph on the fastball there's no diminishment story yet. The honest dependency here is health, a 37-year-old coming off multiple elbow procedures, and the projection calls for meaningful innings — if he stays on the mound, a mid-rotation-to-above-average season is on the table; if he doesn't, nothing else in the profile matters.

reports.name: Ben Brown
reports.published_report: The xwOBA (.280) and xERA (3.22) both land at the 80th percentile, and that's the argument in two numbers: Brown is genuinely suppressing damage, not running on sequencing luck. The fastball sits 96.3 mph, also 80th percentile, and it's clearly doing the heavy lifting, because the chase rate (30.6%) is barely league-average and the strikeout rate (24.5%) is solid without being elite. What makes the profile uncomfortable is the hard-hit rate, 43.0% at the 19th percentile, which means hitters who do connect are connecting well, and the whole thing hinges on whether he can keep limiting barrels (7.3%) as he faces lineups a third time through. If he can, a mid-rotation turn is within reach; if the hard contact catches up, he slides toward a power reliever who posts a very pretty ERA in short stints.

reports.name: Hunter Brown
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument. Brown's Statcast profile reads like a legitimate mid-rotation starter, with a 3.41 xERA, a 27.3% strikeout rate, and an average exit velocity of 85.2 mph that sits at the very top of the leaderboard. The strikeouts get hitters out; the walks put them back on, and a 13.3% walk rate is quietly eating through every margin those numbers build. If the zone command tightens, you've got a genuine front-of-the-rotation contributor posting something close to that projected 3.55 ERA over a full season; if it doesn't, the stuff plays down and he becomes a high-variance arm cycling between brilliance and self-inflicted damage.

reports.name: Francisco Lindor
reports.published_report: The sprint speed tells the story before the bat even speaks: 26.7 ft/s puts Lindor at the 33rd percentile, which means the stolen-base and gap-game version of him has quietly retired. What's left is a shortstop who projects to .239/.322/.410 across 449 plate appearances, solid enough contact and a little pop, but not the dynamic offensive engine that once justified top-of-the-order real estate. The 64th-percentile fielding grade keeps him legitimate at short, so the floor is a useful everyday player rather than a designated-veteran situation. If the bat doesn't inch back toward his better years, the Mets are paying franchise-cornerstone money for a second-division regular in an everyday role.

reports.name: Jeremy Peña
reports.published_report: The xBA of .297 at the 96th percentile tells you almost everything: Peña makes contact at an elite rate for his exit velocity, which sits at just 87.2 mph. That's the whole tension in this profile, a below-average striker of the baseball who somehow generates above-average expected batting averages, because his chase rate at 34.9% and whiff rate at 28.1% don't actually kill him the way they would most hitters. His sprint speed of 29.1 ft/s does real work here, turning soft contact into hits that leave others' hands as outs, and the projection, .280/.339/.430 across 459 PA, is essentially what he is: a legitimate everyday shortstop whose floor is a high-average, low-power regular rather than a middle-of-the-order bat. If the contact skill regresses toward the exit velocity, the SLG stays modest and the profile becomes a platoon conversation; if it holds, he's quietly one of the more dependable offensive shortstops in a lineup that doesn't need him to carry it.

If the contact quality doesn't climb, 16 home runs and a .712 OPS is the realistic ceiling for a full season in Chicago.

reports.name: Clayton Beeter
reports.published_report: Nineteen projected saves out of a bullpen that hasn't had a stable closer in years — that's the argument for Beeter, and it's almost entirely built on one combination. The 95.5 mph fastball is fine, but the 2408 rpm spin sitting at the 83rd percentile is what gives it teeth, the kind of shape that makes a heater play up past its raw number. If the role holds and the command behind that 1.3 WHIP doesn't slip further, a 3.42 ERA closer-by-committee winner is a usable fantasy piece. The whole thing falls apart if Washington installs someone else at the back of the pen, because the underlying stuff supports a late-inning job but doesn't demand one.

reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is bat missing over 49 IP.
reports.published_report: The strikeout stuff is genuine — 11.8 K/9 across AA and A+ this season, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his miss rate at 9.1 against a league that averages 8.6, but the walk rate is the whole argument. His 4.2 BB/9 in the minors translates to 4.0 at the big-league level, a full tick above the 3.2 MLB average, and when the command grade sits at 40, the strikeouts and the walks are essentially canceling each other out. reports.name: Yoendrys Gómez
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is a conflict: 95.4 mph fastball spin at 2449 rpm, sitting in the 86th percentile, attached to a 5.21 xERA. Hitters are barreling him at 11.1% and making hard contact at 43.6%, which explains why the underlying numbers look nothing like the 3.89 ERA ValuCast projects. His 10.4% walk rate compounds the problem — he can't afford contact that heavy when he's also putting runners on for free. Minnesota has him penciled in for 21 saves across 70.778 innings, and if the command tightens and the spin translates into fewer hittable mistakes, the fastball gives him a real closer's weapon; if the contact profile holds, he's a high-leverage gamble who runs into trouble in bunches.

reports.name: Ian Happ
reports.published_report: The 12.9% barrel rate is doing a lot of lifting here, and it's the one number that holds the whole profile together. He chases at just 24.7%, walks at 12.3%, and makes genuine hard contact when he connects — but a 32.1% whiff rate means a lot of at-bats don't connect, and a .203 xBA is a brutal consequence of that. The power is concentrated rather than frequent: the projected .753 OPS over 663 PA is a second-division regular's line, useful at the corner but not a carrying piece. If the strikeouts creep further, you're left with a platoon-adjacent bat that walks too much to bench and doesn't hit enough to start without thinking about it.

reports.name: Devin Williams
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument here. A 36.3% whiff rate and a 38.8% chase rate that almost nobody in the league matches, hitters genuinely cannot make contact when they swing, but a 12.3% BB% that sits near the bottom of the reliever pool drags the projection ERA to 4.06 despite a 3.24 xERA that reflects how little damage he actually surrenders on contact. The Statcast contact profile is dominant; the command is the dependency, and the gap between those two numbers is where the uncertainty lives. If the walks stay at 12.3%, the saves accumulate and the ratios stay frustrating; if he tightens the zone even modestly, the xERA wins and he's one of the more untouchable relievers in the NL.
